The Philippine peso falls below 64 to the dollar despite a surprise rate hike

The Philippine peso closed at 64.17 to the dollar on Tuesday, October 27, a record low. Five days earlier, the central bank had raised its rate by 0.5 point, to 5.5%. Expensive oil and an external deficit are weighing on the currency [1][2][3].

The peso broke through 64 to the dollar for the first time during trading on Tuesday, October 27, then closed at 64.17 against 63.95 the day before, a new record [1][2]. On October 23 it had already hit its 31st low of the year, at 63.615 [6].
On October 22, the central bank (BSP) raised its policy rate by 0.5 point, to 5.5%, its fourth consecutive hike. The 27 economists surveyed by Reuters had expected 0.25 point [3][4].
It is the first 0.5-point hike since February 2023. Governor Eli Remolona says: “we wouldn’t do 50 basis points if we didn’t think we were a bit behind” [4][5].
He also says the bank is not raising its rate to defend the peso [1]. The BSP blames inflation on expensive oil, higher transport costs and El Niño risks [4].
The bank forecasts a balance-of-payments deficit of $9.2 billion and a current account deficit of $19.1 billion in 2026 [1]. It says it is ready to act again [3].

Key point: the Philippines imports a lot of oil, which is paid for in dollars. The more expensive oil is, the more pesos it takes to buy dollars, which weakens the currency [1]. A weak peso in turn makes imports, including fuel, more expensive: this is the imported-inflation cycle [1].
The US Fed also weighs in: the expectation of a rate hike in December is drawing capital toward the dollar [1].

The central bank faces a dilemma: raising rates curbs inflation but slows growth. Remolona says he has estimated how far the peso must move to become inflationary, and that this is when the bank steps in [1][4]. An adviser quoted by a financial website fears a test of the 65-pesos-to-the-dollar level as long as tensions persist [10].

If you travel to the Philippines, the effect depends on the euro’s exchange rate against the dollar. For Filipinos, the bill for fuel and imported goods rises when the peso falls, which feeds inflation [1][4].

Raising the policy rate makes a currency more attractive: foreign investors earn more from it. Bolivia
Bolivia, once a gas powerhouse, allows companies to import it

By a decree dated October 26, Bolivia allows public and private companies to import gas for their own use. Its reserves have shrunk, and authorities warn of a possible shortfall as early as 2029. The country, already shaken by the fuel crisis, must also stick to its IMF program [1][2][3].

Supreme Decree 5755, approved on October 26, authorizes the exceptional import of natural gas and liquefied gas by public and private entities, for their own consumption or to generate electricity. Hydrocarbons Minister Marcelo Blanco specifies that this gas may not be resold on the domestic market [1][2].

Proven reserves stood at about 3.7 trillion cubic feet (TCF) in March 2026, versus 4.5 TCF in 2023, according to the state-owned company YPFB [3]. A new certification, with data as of December 31, 2025, is due out soon; Blanco promises the results within ten days and rules out a gas shortage for domestic consumption [1][3].

Vice Minister Tatiana Genuzio estimates that supply could become insufficient around 2029, when production and demand would converge; YPFB officials speak instead of 2030 or 2031 [2][3]. Gas is heavily subsidized in Bolivia: international prices are nearly ten times higher than local prices, she says [2].

The government attributes the decline to years of insufficient exploration spending under previous governments [2]. Bolivia, long a gas exporter to its neighbors, is thus gradually becoming a buyer, according to the local press [5][6].

At the same time, President Rodrigo Paz scrapped the diesel subsidy on September 19, raising the price per liter from 9.80 to 17.95 bolivianos, after approval of a $1.9 billion IMF loan (confirmed by the IMF board on October 2) [7][8]. The gasoline subsidy is set to end in January 2027 [7].
The state of emergency, declared on June 20 after blockades that cost more than $3 billion according to the press, was extended by 90 days, through December [7][9].

A country that used to sell gas and now has to buy it loses a source of foreign-currency revenue, the one that paid for fuel imports. The government itself links the fuel crisis to falling gas production and costly imports, and President Paz apologized in August for the shortages.

Rodrigo Paz’s government is trying to respond by letting companies fend for themselves with their own imports, and by removing subsidies. But each step hits household budgets, hence the tension with the unions, the COB and the transport operators, who have threatened new protests after the end of the diesel subsidy [7][8].
The uncertainty comes from the numbers: the new reserve certification could shift the date of the “tipping point” [2][3].

If you work for a company that runs mines or factories in Bolivia, or if you follow lithium and tin prices, access to energy becomes an issue. For everyone else, it is an example of what happens when a country lives off gas exports for a long time without investing: the gas its neighbors were buying shrinks.

news.2026-11-01-canada-carney-attendre-n: Canada is ready to wait for another US president rather than sign a bad deal

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he refuses a trade deal with Washington “just to have one” and will wait for a new US president if necessary. Talks have been frozen since August, and each country has added tariffs this fall [1][2][3].

In an interview with Politico in Montreal, published on October 30 or 31 at the end of the 21st EU-Canada summit, Mark Carney said he would not strike a deal “just to get one” and that, asked about having to wait for a new occupant of the White House, he would do so [1].

According to Bloomberg, he hinted that he expects his country to remain in Donald Trump’s sights even after the US elections on November 3. The White House had not responded to requests for comment [1][2].

Negotiations have made little progress since Canada left the table in August [1]. On August 22, after talks collapsed, Washington put in place new 50% tariffs on certain Canadian products, and Carney announced that Canada would respond “dollar for dollar” starting September 8, notably on steel, dairy products, household appliances, farm machinery, paper and electronics [3].
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer had then said that no new talks were planned and that Canada had “refused to finalize” the deal on the terms agreed earlier in the week [3].

On October 29, Ottawa published “The Plan for a Stronger Canada,” a 13-page security strategy: it reiterates the goal of moving toward 5% of GDP for defense (the NATO standard) by 2035, up from 2% in 2025-2026, and promises to “prepare for all contingencies, including war” [6][7].

What is changing is the tone: Canada is no longer seeking a deal at any price before the US elections; it accepts that the conflict may drag on, even outlast Trump. It is a risky political and economic gamble, because the dispute concerns key sectors such as steel and electronics [3].

Carney has room to maneuver at home. On October 19, Albertans rejected the path toward separation from Canada with 74.9% voting against, on a turnout of 70.4% (more than 2.2 million ballots), a result welcomed by Carney and by Alberta Premier Danielle Smith [5].

The country is meanwhile turning to other partners: the summit with the European Union that has just been held in Montreal is proof of it, and the security strategy speaks of “domestic” supply chains and industry [1][6].

Even if you are not in Canada, the trade war between Washington and Ottawa affects the price of steel, aluminum, timber and energy, and therefore what European manufacturers pay. It also pushes Canada to buy its weapons and equipment elsewhere, which may open markets to Europe.

news.2026-11-01-chine-usines-recul-octob: Beijing, China
China
Chinese factories slip into contraction in October as export orders and consumption run out of steam

The official purchasing managers’ index for Chinese manufacturing falls to 49.3 in October, from 50.1 in September, below the 50 threshold that separates growth from contraction. Orders from abroad are shrinking, consumption is falling back, and only high tech is holding up [1][3].

The National Bureau of Statistics published on October 31 a manufacturing PMI (a survey of purchasing managers: above 50, activity is expanding; below it, activity is contracting) of 49.3, versus 50.1 in September and 49.8 in August. A Reuters poll had expected 50.0 [1][4].
It is the third contraction in four months [4]. Output falls to 49.8 (1.9 points lower than in September) and new orders to 49.4 (1.1 points lower) [2].
New export orders fall to 48.7 from 50.0 in September: year-end orders from foreign customers, placed early in September, have faded [1].

Huo Lihui, a statistician at the National Bureau of Statistics, cites purchases brought forward ahead of the National Day holiday at the start of October and a complicated international environment [2]. The consumer goods industry index loses 1.9 points over the month [2].
Services and construction follow: the non-manufacturing index falls to 49.7 from 50.2, and the composite index to 49.7 from 50.7 [3].
High tech is holding up: 51.3 for the high-tech industry and 50.6 for equipment manufacturing, two sectors that are expanding [3].
Zhang Liqun, of the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing, says that “insufficient demand is increasing downward pressure on the economy” [1].
Key point: China can no longer count on foreign sales alone to drive its growth, and its domestic demand remains weak [1][5].

Household purchases rose during the long October holiday week, then fell back right afterward [1]. Economists judge that exports may not be enough to offset consumption that has long been stagnant [5]. Zhang Zhiwei, of Pinpoint Asset Management, says that if external demand weakens in 2027, “China will need greater policy support to revive domestic demand” [1].

Trade relations with Washington remain a source of uncertainty: the truce between the two countries has been extended until January 10, 2027, according to a Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson quoted by a specialist website, but China’s suspension of rare-earth controls has not been confirmed in black and white [6][7].
China is the world’s leading workshop: if its factories order less, the prices of steel, copper or components may ease, but European exporters of machinery and luxury goods sell less there.

Australia: inflation at 4.3%, another rate hike expected Tuesday

Australian inflation reached 4.3% year on year in September, up from 4.0% in August. Markets are now betting overwhelmingly on a rate hike by the central bank (RBA), whose decision is due Tuesday, November 3 [1][3].
The consumer price index rises to 4.3% over twelve months in September, from 4.0% in August [1][2].
The underlying inflation measure (trimmed mean) rose 1.0% over the quarter and 3.7% year on year, above the 3.6% expected [2].

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese attributes the inflation partly to higher oil prices and the conflict in the Middle East, while acknowledging that bringing it down remains a challenge [1].
The RBA board meets on November 2 and 3, with an announcement on the 3rd [4][5]. Depending on the source, the probabilities of a hike range from 73% to 90%, so nothing is settled [2][3].
